results.summary: This design implements a small UART transmitter that repeatedly sends a fixed string (the author's name) at 115200 baud with one start bit, eight data bits, one parity bit and one stop bit. It also generates a sinus signal on the remaining seven output pins. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and no inputs; testing only needs a UART receiver connected to uo_out[0]. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the behavior and pin usage.

This project implements a 1-bit 8x8 matrix multiply using a systolic array, with eight data input pins and eight output pins for the result. A bidirectional pin selects between OR and XOR accumulation, and another bidirectional pin outputs a greeting. The documentation consists only of placeholder text ('Explain how your project works' and 'Explain how to test your project'), so the exact interface and operation cannot be verified beyond the pin names and title. The design is notable for targeting matrix multiplication in a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

This SystemVerilog design implements a UART transceiver with both transmit and receive functions at 9600 baud, using oversampling to sample the middle of each bit period. The receiver waits for a start bit, samples eight data bits and a stop bit, and asserts a data-ready signal; the transmitter sends a byte with correct timing when a data-ready input is set. The eight output pins double as 7-segment display segments and as the UART transmit data output, while bidirectional pins carry received data and a finished-read flag. Testing requires setting the data bits and data-ready input and observing the transmitted sequence on the tx output.

This design is a 12-hour clock rendered on a 640x480 VGA display using a race-the-beam triangle renderer, where three triangle hands indicate the time and twelve dots aid readability. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a 31.5 MHz clock, reset, and hour and minute advance buttons. Silicon test reports confirm it works out of the box with a Tiny VGA Pmod, with testers noting the hands move correctly and the time can be set by holding the buttons. The design is notable for its triangle-based rendering approach and includes a Rust software model for reference.

This design is described as a hardcoded perceptron, but the documentation actually describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal counter that increments once per second with a 10 MHz clock. The eight output pins carry the perceptron output, while the inputs can be used to program a 24-bit compare register to change the counting speed. The documentation is inconsistent with the title, and the perceptron behavior is not explained. Testing involves observing the counter increment and changing the input bits to alter the rate.

This project implements a perceptron and a basic binary neural network that take a 7-bit input representing the number of curves and edges of a digit and output the expected number. The eight output pins drive a 7-segment display plus a dot, and the bidirectional pins expose a second counter. The documentation is largely copied from a counter project and does not explain the neural network operation or how to test it meaningfully. The design appears to be a class project, but the documentation is insufficient to verify its intended behavior.

This design implements a perceptron that reads two 8-bit inputs and computes a weighted sum with fixed 8-bit weights, classifying the result as 1 if it exceeds a threshold of 11111110 and 0 otherwise. The documentation explains the math with examples, such as any input with two or more 1s being classified as 1, and credits a UCSC professor. It is intended as a simple 9+10 adder or perceptron demonstration, and testing involves applying inputs and observing the 8-bit output. The design is notable for being an educational neuromorphic example with clear documentation.

This design implements a Boolean function based pseudo random number generator using finite field arithmetic, with linear mappings, GF(2^4) multipliers, an inverter, and a square scaler. It takes five input bytes as seeds and produces three output shares, using masking with fresh randomness to prevent leakage. The documentation provides a detailed mathematical description of the three phases and a worked example, and testing involves loading input shares, toggling the enable signal, and reading the output ready flag and shares. The design is notable for its cryptographic masking approach and is implemented in a 1x2 tile configuration.

This project implements a bytebeat formula in hardware using the XLS toolkit, generating 8-bit PCM samples from four 4-bit parameters according to the formula ((t*a)&(t>>b))|((t*c)&(t>>d)). It requires an 8-bit PCM DAC and rotary encoders to tweak the parameter pins, and the design can be modified by editing the formula and regenerating the Verilog. A silicon test report from the author confirms it worked as expected after configuring the bidirectional mode correctly. The design is notable for being generated from a high-level synthesis tool and for bringing algorithmic music synthesis to Tiny Tapeout.

This design is a guitar tuner that counts rising edges of an input pulse over a fixed sampling period and compares the count to frequencies of interest for standard guitar tuning, covering notes from about 80 to 400 Hz. It supports multiple clock configurations via three input bits and can drive either a dual or single 7-segment display, with the dot indicating an exact match in single mode. The raw pulse count is output on the bidirectional pins, and testing requires feeding a variable frequency signal and observing the closest note on the display. A silicon test report confirms it works, showing the closest note for a variable frequency input.
